title: 米大統領 金正恩氏と会談の可能性
body: [ワシントン １６日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は１６日、今週の‌アジア歴訪中に北朝鮮の金⁠正恩朝鮮労働党総書記と会談する可能性があると​の認識を示した。実現すれば、大統領の歴訪日程‌が大きく変更される可能性もある。トランプ大統領は、フ‌ィリピンと中‌国に向かうためホワイ​トハウスを出発する前、記者団‌に対し、中国の習近平国家主席が「１カ月前‌にここを​訪れた。われわれは（ロシ‌アの）プーチン大統領とも会談する。⁠金氏とも会談するかもしれない」と語り、「それは良いこと⁠だ。多くのことを成し​遂げるチ‌ャンスがある」と語った。さらに、金氏との会談は中国で行われる⁠可能性があり、最終的には⁠習氏次第だと述べた。習氏とプーチン氏⁠との会談では、ウクライナ情勢や核‌不拡⁠散、イラン問題、経済、貿​易について協議するとの考えを示した。

title: 「防衛産業基盤戦略」概要が判明
body:
政府が、安全保障３文書の改定に合わせて年内に策定する「防衛産業基盤戦略」の概要が判明した。官民一体で支援する法人を新設し、防衛装備品の輸出促進に向け、企業から装備品を買い取って相手国との窓口となる役割を担わせる。米政府の制度にならった「日本版ＦＭＳ（対外有償軍事援助）」と位置づける。【図】一目でわかる…自衛隊は四方八方に目を光らせている
複数の政府関係者が明らかにした。防衛産業基盤戦略では、装備品輸出について「同盟国・同志国との連携強化の重要な手段で、予備生産力の確保や有事の相互融通など継戦能力の強化の観点から極めて重要」だと強調する。
安保上重要で民間企業のみでの輸出が困難な装備品については、新法人が買い取って相手国に輸出する日本版ＦＭＳで対応すると明記する。風評リスクを懸念する企業があり、政府が正面に出るよう求める声が上がっていた。ＦＭＳは、米政府が自国製の武器を同盟国や友好国の政府に有償で提供する仕組みだ。
新法人が中心となって相手国向けの教育訓練や部品の現地製造などをパッケージで支援する取り組みも掲げる。国家安全保障局を中心とした司令塔組織を設立し、関係省庁や新法人が連携して後押しする。
生産基盤の強化に向けては、企業の設備投資を促すため、防衛産業と防衛省幹部による対話の枠組みを設ける。将来の防衛構想を協議し、企業が中長期の計画を立てやすくする。有事の増産体制を築くための財政支援制度や、研究人材を確保するための拠点を大学などに設置する方針も盛り込む。

title: ケーキ店死傷 死亡の男を書類送検
body:
9月に岐阜県本巣市のケーキ店から出火し、店主らが亡くなるなどした事件で、県警は17日、店主ら3人を殺害し、7人を殺害しようとしたとして、殺人や現住建造物等放火などの疑いで、現場から病院搬送後に死亡した葬祭業林寛至容疑者＝当時（70）、同県瑞穂市＝を容疑者死亡のまま書類送検した。【動画】ケーキ店火災、3人死亡　岐阜、殺人と放火で捜査
書類送検容疑は、ケーキ店で9月5日夜、福田達哉さん＝同（66）＝の腹部を包丁で刺して殺害した後、ガソリンをまいて火を付け、店主の曽野さとみさん＝同（66）＝と堀部真由美さん＝同（65）＝を殺害し、7人を殺害しようとした疑い。県警によると、現場の店舗兼住宅には事件当時、曽野さんと同窓会グループの計10人と、林容疑者がいた。

title: 菊地直子さん 逃亡の日々振り返る
body: 指名手配されたまま、身分を偽って生きた17年。菊地直子さん（54）は逮捕のあと、裁かれた事件では無罪が確定した。それでも「走る爆弾娘」の名は剥がれず、ネットの言葉が彼女を追い詰めた。寝込みながらも、手記を書き上げるまでに3年余り。逃げ続けた日々と、いまを生き直そうとする姿を、本人の言葉でたどった。【写真】逃亡中だった30代半ばの頃の菊地直子さん*　　　*　　　*「本当の意味で、安らげることはなかったと思います」菊地直子さん（54）は、静かに振り返る。1995年3月20日朝、東京都内を走る地下鉄3路線の車内に猛毒のサリンがほぼ同時に散布され、乗客や乗員ら14人が死亡、約6300人が重軽傷を負った。オウム真理教が引き起こした地下鉄サリン事件だ。菊地さんは、この教団の信者だった。事件から約2カ月後の95年5月、殺人と殺人未遂の容疑で教団関係者ら41人に逮捕状が出た。23歳だった菊地さんもその一人で、特別指名手配された。ここから、17年に及ぶ逃亡生活が始まった。市川市（千葉県）、名古屋市、京都市、所沢市（埼玉県）など各地を元信者たちと転々とした。96年末には所沢を離れ、同じく元信者の高橋克也氏（2018年に無期懲役が確定）と川崎市（神奈川県）に逃げ、ともに暮らした。実在する他人の住民票を取って使い、偽名で働いた。派遣社員として、倉庫でのライン作業や物流会社でのピッキング作業に就いた。スーパーの寿司コーナーで働いたこともあった。やがて、派遣先の物流会社で知り合った男性と交際。07年3月に高橋氏のもとを離れ、男性と町田市（東京都）のアパートに移った。その後、相模原市（神奈川県）に転居した。身分を偽って社会に紛れる日々。いつ正体を知られ、逮捕されるかわからない緊張の連続だった。「毎日が必死でした。仕事と生活、そして逃げることに追われ、その日をなんとか無事に終わらせるのが精いっぱいでした」

title: 「白い麻婆豆腐」じわじわ拡大
body: 専門店も続々登場し人気が高まる「麻婆豆腐」に、今“ある変化”が起きています。■「お出汁が香る」あっさりコク旨【写真で見る】「変幻自在」…白い麻婆豆腐　レトルトも続々「えっ! 麻婆豆腐なのに白い。辛くない!」中華ファミリーレストラン『バーミヤン』でこの秋から登場したのは、色だけでなく味も変わった「コク旨!白い麻婆豆腐〜海老・中華クワイ・山芋入り〜」（879円）THE TIME,マーケティング部　国本梨紗部員:「すごく優しい“お出汁の香り”がする。あまり辛みは感じなくて、代わりに山椒のシビれる感覚がある。こんなに違うんだ」一般的な麻婆豆腐は豆板醤を炒め、醤油や味噌ベースで味付けをしますが、白い麻婆豆腐は「豆板醤を使わず」、味付けには「白醤油や2種類の花椒」を使用。さらに、麻婆豆腐ではなかなか使わない“シャキシャキ食感”の野菜「中華クワイ」、揚げた海老、山芋と食感を楽しめる具材もゴロゴロ入っていて、すでにリピーターも多いといいます。▼30代女性:「実はちょっとハマっていて、今日で5回目くらい」▼50代男性:「辛さが控えめですごく食べやすい。今度は食べ比べセットを食べてみようかな」当初は期間限定の予定でしたが、あまりの人気ぶりに「グランドメニューでの継続販売」も決定しています。■「キノコの旨味」でごはんが進む行列ができる専門店にも“白の波”が来ています。黒・白・赤・黄・炎と5種類の麻婆豆腐が選べる『麻婆豆腐TOKYO 神田本店』（東京・千代田区）で最近人気が急上昇なのが「白 うま塩麻婆豆腐」（1180円※ランチ価格）『麻婆豆腐TOKYO』創業者・大久保俊祐さん:「発酵調味料が入らない中で旨みを出すのがすごく難しくて、個性が出るように食材も考えた。春から特に人気が高まっていて売り上げは1.5倍ほど」鶏肉とマッシュルームの旨みを出したスープにごま油で香りづけ。シンプルながらもご飯に合う白い麻婆豆腐です。国本部員:「ごま油のすごくいい香り。ベースは塩味ですごくあっさりしているけど出汁がしっかり効いていておいしい。最高」

title: 米中露 共同コミュニケを発表へ
body: ロシアのウシャコフ大統領補佐官は16日、中国・深センで19日に開かれる史上初の米中ロ首脳会談後、共同コミュニケが発表される見通しだと明らかにした。【ひと目でわかる】米中ロ朝の関係3者会談は「第2次大戦での3カ国の相互理解と同盟関係を考慮し、国連創設における各国の協力に重点を置いて組み立てられる」と強調。戦後秩序の中核を担う「戦勝国」としての立場をアピールした形だ。中国外務省はこれより先、3カ国が「かつて肩を並べて戦い、世界反ファシズム戦争（第2次大戦）で勝利した」と主張した。関係が悪化している日本をけん制する狙いがあるとみられている。3者会談は18、19両日に深センで行われるアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に合わせて実施する。トランプ米大統領によれば、核軍備管理のほか、イランやウクライナの情勢が議題に上る。ウシャコフ氏は、共同コミュニケの文案が「難しい外交交渉の中で形になりつつある」と指摘。まとまらなければ、各首脳が会談後、それぞれの立場を説明するという。同氏は、トランプ氏とロシアのプーチン大統領の個別会談が「100％行われる」と断言。ウクライナ和平が議題になる見通しで、日程は調整中だという。米政府高官は、プーチン氏との個別会談は予定されていないとしていた。プーチン氏は18日、中国の習近平国家主席と会談する。習氏に対し、アラブ首長国連邦（UAE）で行われた米ロ・ウクライナの3カ国実務者協議などを踏まえ、米側との最近のやりとりについて伝える。

title: 3カ国会談巡り中国「戦勝国」強調
body: 19日に中国・深圳市で開かれる史上初の米中露首脳会談を巡り、中国外務省の毛寧報道局長は16日の記者会見で「世界平和や大国関係の戦略的安定について深く意見を交わす」と表明。さらに「歴史上、3カ国は世界反ファシスト戦争（第二次世界大戦）で共に勝利した」と述べ、戦後秩序を主導する「戦勝国」の地位をアピールする意図を鮮明にした。【図解】トランプ氏、プーチン氏、習近平氏　３人の思惑は中国は、悲願とする台湾統一を「第二次大戦における勝利の成果」と位置づけ、高市早苗政権を「新型軍国主義」と批判してきた。ロシアのプーチン大統領は歴史問題で中国と共闘しており、日本の北方領土を「戦勝国の成果」と見なしている。習近平国家主席が9月に訪米した際、トランプ米大統領から「米中は大戦の同盟国」との発言を引き出しており、ロシアを加えた今回の3カ国会談でも「米中露は戦勝国」と打ち出すことが大きな狙いとみられる。史上初の米中露首脳会談は、深圳市で18～19日に開かれるアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に合わせて開かれる。米国が先行して開催を認めていたが、中国外務省も16日に正式に発表。毛氏はその意義について「中露米が意思疎通を深め、安定した関係を強化することは国際社会の期待にかなう」と強調した。【北京・河津啓介】

title: イラン「汚い爆弾」米高官狙いか
body: （CNN）　イランがトランプ米政権の高官を狙って首都ワシントンで「汚い爆弾」の使用を計画している兆候があるとして、米国が警戒を強めている。ただ、イランにそうした計画の実行を試みる能力や意思があるのかどうかについては、米当局者の間でも論議が続いているという。7人の米当局者がCNNに明らかにした。【映像】イラン、地下トンネルに並ぶドローンの映像公開最新情報に詳しい関係者はイランのこの計画について、現時点では差し迫った攻撃の兆候というよりも、選択肢を増やすための取り組みと形容した。ただ、米情報機関がつかんだ同計画に関する情報は場所や標的も含まれるなど極めて具体的で、米国側は急きょ緊急時の対応計画に乗り出したという。ホワイトハウスのローレン・ビス報道官は、「潜在的脅威は全て監視している。だが現時点で、米本土に対する信憑（しんぴょう）性の高い脅威は存在しない」とコメントした。しかし米当局者は今回の情報を、イランが事態をエスカレートさせようとしていることを示す憂慮すべき兆候と受け止めている。イランは現在、米軍による攻撃と、米政権が「壊滅的」と形容する厳しい経済封鎖によって強い圧力にさらされている。たとえイランが計画の実行を決断したという証拠はなかったとしても、そうした情報があること自体、イランが現在、米国内で攻撃を実行する計画を積極的に立案していることの表れだと関係者は指摘する。関係者の1人は「イランが実際に、実行のための要員を配置しているかどうかについては論議が分かれる」とした。「汚い爆弾」は放射性物質を通常の爆弾に仕込んだ兵器で、比較的簡単に製造できる。米国はそうした非通常兵器に対して極めて脆弱（ぜいじゃく）な状況にあるとして、当局者は警戒を強めている。

title: 米大統領 金正恩氏と会談の可能性
body: [ワシントン １６日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は１６日、今週の‌アジア歴訪中に北朝鮮の金⁠正恩朝鮮労働党総書記と会談する可能性があると​の認識を示した。実現すれば、大統領の歴訪日程‌が大きく変更される可能性もある。トランプ大統領は、フ‌ィリピンと中‌国に向かうためホワイ​トハウスを出発する前、記者団‌に対し、中国の習近平国家主席が「１カ月前‌にここを​訪れた。われわれは（ロシ‌アの）プーチン大統領とも会談する。⁠金氏とも会談するかもしれない」と語り、「それは良いこと⁠だ。多くのことを成し​遂げるチ‌ャンスがある」と語った。さらに、金氏との会談は中国で行われる⁠可能性があり、最終的には⁠習氏次第だと述べた。習氏とプーチン氏⁠との会談では、ウクライナ情勢や核‌不拡⁠散、イラン問題、経済、貿​易について協議するとの考えを示した。

title: トランプ大統領 アジア歴訪へ出発
body: 【ワシントン時事】トランプ米大統領は16日、アジア歴訪に出発した。中国・深センでは19日、史上初の米中ロ首脳会談を実施。今年3回目となる中国の習近平国家主席との会談も行う。大国外交で国際政治を主導するかのような動きを「第2のヤルタ会談」と警戒する声も上がっている。【ひと目でわかる】米中ロ朝の関係トランプ氏は、フィリピン・マニラで東南アジア諸国連合（ASEAN）関連会合、深センではアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に出席する。ただ、国際協調に後ろ向きなトランプ氏にとって、国際会議よりも個別の首脳会談が優先事項だ。米中ロ首脳は核軍備管理を議論する予定。米国の対イラン軍事作戦やロシアによるウクライナ侵攻も協議するという。トランプ氏は、自身が望む軍備管理を議題にする代わりに、台湾やウクライナを巡って中ロに譲歩する可能性がある。ただ、いずれも3者の思惑は異なり、「メディアの前での写真撮影以上の成果はない」（ジョージ・メイソン大のマーク・キャッツ名誉教授）と冷ややかな見方も多い。米中首脳会談では、人工知能（AI）のリスク管理に加え、関税の一部や輸出規制の強化などを停止する貿易戦争の「休戦」期限の延長、中国による米産農産物の輸入などが議題になる見通し。トランプ氏と習氏は昼食も共にする。中ロの指導者に融和的な姿勢を強めるトランプ氏に、同盟国の間で懸念が広がっている。ただ、トランプ氏はマニラで17日、日米とオーストラリア、インドの4カ国の連携枠組み「クアッド」首脳会合に参加する。米政府高官は「クアッドは、自由で開かれたインド太平洋を確保するための機会を推進している」と強調する。また、18日には、南シナ海で中国と領有権争いを抱えるフィリピンのマルコス大統領とも会談する。同盟国や友好国との連携を示すことで、米中ロ会談の前に最低限の配慮を見せた格好だ。

title: NY株大幅反落 ハイテク株に売り
body:
【ニューヨーク共同】週明け16日のニューヨーク株式市場のダウ工業株30種平均は大幅反落し、前週末比739.38ドル安の5万1608.17ドルで取引を終えた。半導体大手エヌビディアを巡る先行き懸念などから、ハイテク株を中心に売り注文が膨らんだ。【画像】キオクシアの株価が半値に下落　ストップ安、投資家が警戒感　7月
エヌビディアは、ベセント米財務長官による経営刷新要求や、対中半導体規制が売り材料視された。取締役会がファン前最高経営責任者（CEO）の復帰を否定したと伝わったことも、マイナス要因として意識された。ハイテク株主体のナスダック総合指数は3営業日続落し、626.51ポイント安の2万4509.76だった。他の個別銘柄では、建設機械のキャタピラー、ITのアルファベットの下落が目立った。家庭用品のプロクター・アンド・ギャンブル（P＆G）は買われた。

title: フアン氏復帰求める署名 16万人超
body: 中国のスパイと疑われる女性や部下との不倫関係が報じられた後、CEOを辞任したエヌビディアのジェンスン・フアン氏が、復帰を検討していると報じられました。【画像】中国スパイと報じられたアリス・フアン氏イギリスのフィナンシャル・タイムズは15日、関係者の話として、フアン氏が側近らとCEOに復帰する可能性について協議していると報じました。フアン氏の復帰を後押しするシリコンバレーの経営者らは、「作戦本部」を設け、エヌビディアの取締役会に働きかけるほか、ホワイトハウスの支持も取り付けようとしているということです。こうした動きは、フアン氏本人も支持しているとしています。一方、ベッセント財務長官は15日、エヌビディアには抜本的な刷新が必要だとして、後任のCEOは社外から起用すべきだとの考えを示しました。フィナンシャル・タイムズは、フアン氏を復帰させようとする動きは、アメリカ政界から強い反発を受ける可能性があると指摘しています。一方、インターネットではフアン氏の復帰を求める署名活動も行われ、署名サイトによりますとこれまでに16万人を超えていて実業家のイーロン・マスク氏らも賛同しています。エヌビディアとフアン氏側は、復帰の動きについてコメントしていません。

title: タイムズカーの会員数 1.4万人減
body:
貸駐車場大手のパーク24は16日、カーシェアリングサービス「タイムズカー」の10月末時点の会員数が前月比0.3％減の421万2千人だったと発表した。9月末時点から1万4千人減った。パーク24によると、9月下旬に公表した不正アクセスによる運転免許証画像などの流出が影響した。【写真】タイムズ流出に3千円の見舞金　免許画像146万件の漏えい確認
2009年5月のサービス開始以降、月次ベースで会員数が減少するのは初めて。パーク24は9月28日にタイムズカーへの不正アクセスで、個人情報が流出したと公表。調査の結果、外部送信の痕跡を確認した運転免許証画像のデータは延べ約146万人分だった。

title: マンション短期売買 課税強化検討
body: 都心部のマンション価格の高騰に歯止めをかけようと、政府・与党が投機的な取引を抑えるための課税強化の検討に入った。短期間で転売して利益を得る取引が価格高騰の一因になっているとみて、所得税や不動産取得税などを増税する案が浮上している。12月にまとめる2027年度の税制改正大綱に盛り込む方向で、具体的な制度設計を詰める。予算7千万円「この値段でこれか」　マンション高騰個人が不動産を売却して得た利益には、期間が5年以下なら所得税と住民税を合わせて約40%、5年超なら約20%が課される。これを5年以下の区分をさらに細分化し、1～3年以内を設けるなど、より短期間で売却した場合の税率を引き上げる案がある。投機的な土地取引を抑える目的で創設され、バブル崩壊後の1998年から適用を停止している土地譲渡益への税金を重くする制度を一部活用することも検討されている。新築マンションを短期間で転売した場合、不動産取得税の軽減措置の対象から外す案もある。ただ、転勤などの事情で短期間で自宅を手放すケースもあり、投機目的の短期売買と実需に基づく取引をどう区別するかが課題だ。

title: いきステに復活の兆し 改革の成果
body:
「いきなり！ステーキ」を展開するペッパーフードサービスが、復活の兆しを見せている。
11月13日発表の2026年12月期第3四半期累計（1～9月）は、売上高が前年同期比13.6％増の122億100万円。営業損益は前年同期の9100万円の赤字から2億300万円の黒字へ転換した。通期黒字なら3年連続となる。
かつて急拡大で一世を風靡したが、業績悪化で大量閉店を余儀なくされた同社。2022年には創業者の一瀬邦夫氏から長男の健作氏へ経営を引き継いだ。社長交代から約4年、改革の成果が着実に数字に表れている。

title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
body:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by theincoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the plan to open a centre in Rwanda had no "future or humanity", according to AFP news agency.
"I don't see any future or humanity in that. It's not the solution," Sanchez told the Spanish broadcaster Telecinco, AFP reported.
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had amajor role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would bea cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

title: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are gaining ground and their advance could have dangerous consequences, writes the BBC's security correspondent.
body:
What happens next in Yemen may send fresh shockwaves to the world economy
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.
But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?
When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.
The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.
But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.
On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.
Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."
He warns that if the port of Aden – a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants – was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."
It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.
The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.
"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO
summary: A number of tech figures have backed an effort asking the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
body:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week followingrevelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis forone of the world's most valuable firms- a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants,according to the Financial Times,external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huangsince the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of ameeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.
The interim ruleswill require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.
The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.
He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".
In 2025, Nvidia wonan approval to sell some advanced AI chipsin China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level ofscrutiny over deals abroad.
The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.
Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.
But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.
But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to  companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.
US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, includingbefore the House Select Committee on Chinato discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,"he posted on X.,external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself wasreinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023,said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officerColette Kress is leading the firmand will present the company's results on Tuesday.

title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
summary: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.
body:
The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
summary: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.
body:
Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.
Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.
His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.
But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".
Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.
The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits.
By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support.
In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:
A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028)
More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum
Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis
A doubling of the number of young apprentices
Incentives for employers, such aslowering the National Insurance rate for young workers
At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.
The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.
To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.
The review's key welfare measures, some of which havealready been announced, suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.
The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.
Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.
She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.
Kat says her health issues limit her ability to find work
Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.
Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.
Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".
Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".
Josh has been looking for work for three years
Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.
The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.
So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.
The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.
It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.
Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".
Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".
She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".
Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap".
"Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.
For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges OpenAI misled and endangered the public
body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026attack on the AI platform Hugging Faceby experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

title: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs
summary: How many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?
body:
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.
Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.
But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?
There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in the July to September period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.
The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.
Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.
Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.
In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.
The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a recent peak of 291,300 in 2012.
Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.
We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.
The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.
According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.
Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.
Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.
The sector with the highest average number ofentry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.
The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.
Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.
Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.
Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead ofplans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.
Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.

title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
summary: People who can't afford to get on the housing ladder are buying homes with people they don't know.
body:
The Pullman family, on the left, and the Wilcox family, bought a home together soon after meeting
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.
The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along
While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.
It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".
"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."
The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.
Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.
While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.
She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."
They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.
"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.
Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication
In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.
For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.
Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.
Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.
"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO
summary: A number of tech figures have backed an effort asking the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
body:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week followingrevelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis forone of the world's most valuable firms- a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.
Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".
Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants,according to the Financial Times,external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huangsince the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.
The move comes ahead of ameeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.
The interim ruleswill require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.
The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.
He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".
In 2025, Nvidia wonan approval to sell some advanced AI chipsin China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level ofscrutiny over deals abroad.
The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.
Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.
But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.
But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to  companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry.
US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, includingbefore the House Select Committee on Chinato discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,"he posted on X.,external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself wasreinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023,said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officerColette Kress is leading the firmand will present the company's results on Tuesday.

title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
summary: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.
body:
Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.
Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.
His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.
But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".
Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.
The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits.
By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support.
In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:
A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028)
More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum
Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis
A doubling of the number of young apprentices
Incentives for employers, such aslowering the National Insurance rate for young workers
At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.
The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.
To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.
The review's key welfare measures, some of which havealready been announced, suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.
The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.
Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.
She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.
Kat says her health issues limit her ability to find work
Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.
Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.
Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".
Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".
Josh has been looking for work for three years
Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.
The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.
So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.
The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.
It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.
Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".
Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".
She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".
Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap".
"Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.
For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

title: Children dropping out of school: What can politicians do about it?
summary: The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be not in education, employment or training.
body:
'It felt like I was dying’: Why some teenagers don’t go to school
The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address.
The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet.
A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence.
The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent.
Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9.
Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school
Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.
She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.
Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10.
We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be.
It offers an insight into the political arguments to come.
Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down.
A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve."
Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support".
The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories.
Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong".
These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences.
Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision?
Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides.
The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back.
"Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools."
And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet."
Former Conservative cabinet minister Suella Braverman, now Reform UK's education spokesperson, told us: "As someone who co-founded and chaired an outstanding state school with a high proportion of children on free school meals but a below average school absence rate, it is clear that the culture and teaching in a school can make a huge difference."
She added that "greater parental engagement" and a "culture of perseverance" were essential too.
The government is expected to accept the broad thrust of Alan Milburn's report, before responding in detail in the next month or so.
We are told there will be an announcement from Education Secretary Lucy Powell directly relevant to Eva, Mali and the many like them, later this week.

title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
summary: The gender care review author says the bill’s wording risks "serious unintended consequences" for parents and therapists.
body:
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".
Conversion practicesare generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced itsdraft legislation,externalin June this year, Baroness Cass wasquoted in the publicity for it,external.
In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.
The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.
"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.
She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.
She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.
Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
When she published herreport on gender identity servicesfor young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.
She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."
The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.
"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.
"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."
The committee hearings continue.

title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
summary: Under proposed new rules, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove a person without telling them in advance.
body:
The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.
Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.
Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.
The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."
Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.
"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.
The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.
Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.
The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.
The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.
In June 2026, there were 40,168 people waiting for an initial decision on asylum application claims and a further 90,341 waiting for the outcome of an appeal in the courts.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, 38% of asylum decisions led to the applicant being granted refugee status.
Forty percent of all asylum claims come from people who arrived in the UK by small boat.
The remaining 60% of claims are made by people who arrived in the country by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and subsequently applied for asylum.
Anna Turley, minister for border security and asylum, said: "We are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.
"This bill will restore order and control to the system, ensuring it is swift and fair."

title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit
summary: The prime minister tells an audience at the Lord Mayor's Banquet that the "Brexit we were given has not worked".
body:
Watch: 'Hard Brexit we were given not good enough for Britain,' says Burnham
The prime ministerhas argued the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.
Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnhamcompared the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.
He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, after the substance of those deals was set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door".
In his first major speech on foreign policy, the prime minister said that following the summit he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for "our long-term relationship".
However, he warned it would take time and insisted that "at every stage the British people will be the boss".
Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election.
On the UK's current relationship with EU, Burnham said: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."
Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham set out three tests for any agreement.
Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".
He also said it must improve the original Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
Finally, he said any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives - a reference to voters in Burnham's Greater Manchester constituency.
He also said the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".
"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."
Burnham said "Britain was back in the game in a big way" and would be a country that "leads with its values".

This week's summit will see the UK seek to agree further changes to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's deal, struck in May 2025, covering fishing, trade and other areas.
The UK and EU have agreed adraft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exportsahead of the meeting.
The government argues the agreement will help cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.
However, critics say the deal will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels, aligning with EU regulations without being able to vote on them.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.
These deals were close to being finalised under Sir Keir, with only some details still to be worked out.

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnhamhad promised not to "re-run" Brexit argumentsand said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".
However, since becoming prime minister he has said he wants to explore a different long-term relationship with the bloc.
He has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.
The prime minister has stressed any changes would require a mandate from the public at a general election.
Boris Johnson, who was prime minister when the UK left the EU in 2020 and negotiated the original Brexit deal, has warned Burnham against "wasting his premiership" on Europe.
He told the Daily Telegraph,externalhe believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
"It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority," Johnson told the paper.
"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."
Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart accused Burnham of "reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today".
Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.
The Liberal Democrats have said the draft deal on food exports is a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".
The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".
